title: Topology surgery: VPC egress, NAT tradeoffs, KV cache & batching simulation
summary: Hands-on deep dive to map AtlasStream's private VPC design to Redwood Private. Covered tradeoffs between central NAT vs per-az NAT, PrivateLink architectures, split-horizon DNS for resolver paths, and how KV cache and batching interact with networking latency. Agreed next steps to run controlled perf sims and share a network/runbook artifact.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-04 16:00 UTC
Duration approx: 75 minutes
Attendees: Samir (AE, Redwood), Priya (SE, Redwood), John (Infra, AtlasStream), Leah (Platform, AtlasStream), Rajesh (Security, AtlasStream)

Summary:
- Quick intro then jumped into egress topology options, NAT scaling and DNS routing. Discussed how KV cache hot-keys amplify latency when egress hops are high.

Topics:
- Egress NAT topologies
- PrivateLink vs cross-account peering
- DNS resolver split-horizon and route53 / conditional forwarding
- KV cache eviction patterns and batching window sizing
- Quantization impact on tail latency
- mTLS cert rotation and SNI config for PrivateLink

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood): ok thanks team, welcome everyone, we wanted to do a surgery on your topology and run a couple of mental sims. quick intro if you can state role real quick
[00:10] John (AtlasStream): john, infra, we run most of our workloads in us-east-1, three private subnets, single nat gw today, and we saw tail jumps when bursts hit
[00:22] Leah (AtlasStream): leah, platform, primarily interested in p99/95 latency and costs — want to know if we should move to dedicated per-az nat or use privatelink for redd- run inference calls
[00:37] Priya (Redwood SE): cool, thanks. couple of framing q's: what is your request size distribution? are you mainly streaming responses or short sync calls?
[00:45] John: mostly short sync calls, 80% under 512 tokens, but we do have batch generation for larger reports, and we reuse k v cache heavily for multi-turn flows
[01:03] Samir: k v as in k-v cache for transformer key/value cache, the small 2-step reuse right?
[01:08] John: yeah sorry the transcript thing, we say "kay vee" sometimes, but yes the model cache, and we've got hot keys — a small percent of users generate lots of requests which concentrates cache hits
[01:25] Priya: got it. primary tradeoff: central nat is cheap operationally but you get hairpinning and single egress hop which can balloon p99 during spikes. per-az nat reduces cross-az hops but costs more. private link avoids nat for control-plane calls but you still need outbound resolver and sometimes egress for model registries
[02:00] Leah: can you explain the private link flow? we worry about cross-account privatelink latency and TLS behaviour
[02:10] Priya: sure. PrivateLink gives you an ENI in your subnet. traffic to the service stays within AWS fabric; you avoid nat. but you need to design for SNI and mTLS: the service needs to accept the certs, and if you have split-horizon DNS you must ensure the resolver returns the VPC endpoint address when inside the VPC
[02:40] Rajesh (Security): and about mTLS rotation — do you have an automated rotation pattern? we need certs to rotate without downtime
[02:50] Samir: we do; Redwood supports cert rotation via our control plane, you can pre-stage certs and do a rolling rotate, also we can recommend TTLs that work with your DNS caches
[03:10] John: our current DNS is forwarded to resolver at 10.2.0.2 which then forwards to the ISP in nat. if we switch to privatelink, would we avoid that? how does split-horizon play?
[03:24] Priya: you need a resolver that resolves the redwood domain to the endpoint ip inside the VPC. AWS Route 53 private hosted zones or a conditional forwarder to AWS resolver works. watch out for timeouts — some resolvers can add 40-80ms overhead if misconfigured
[03:48] Leah: that sounds like it could hit our p95
[03:52] Priya: yes, so we recommend warm resolver caches, lower TTLs for dev but higher for prod, and pre-warming the KV cache when doing canaries
[04:10] Samir: speaking of KV cache, we ran a little sim last week: when the network RTT to the backend model increases by 20ms, hot-key misses in the KV cache amplified p99 by ~30% because batches started to pile up waiting on the same keys
[04:30] John: interesting — so network jitter maps to longer head of queue
[04:35] Priya: exactly. the runtime does continuous batching, so if a hot key stalls outgoing requests, subsequent requests pile behind it. mitigation is twofold: reduce per-request dependency on single-key locks and tune batching windows (max batch size and max batch delay)
[05:00] Samir: another practical knob is to shard the KV cache across nodes to reduce lock contention, but that increases cross-node communication — so if your network topology forces cross-az hops it may be worse
[05:18] John: would per-az cache shards be better? we already have per-az compute
[05:24] Priya: yes, per-az shards are usually best if you can avoid cross-az egress. If you go with a central nat and a single KV plane, you'll see higher tail. for AtlasStream we think per-az shard + privatelink for control-plane + selective nat for internet dependencies is a good middle ground
[05:45] Leah: curious about batching sizing — we saw a reg where larger batches lowered token cost but increased p99 significantly
[05:55] Priya: that's the typical tradeoff. For short token distributions you want small max_batch_delay (e.g., 5-15ms) and reasonable max_batch_size (8-32). For long-run jobs you can route them to dedicated capacity with higher batch sizes. also quantization interacts: int8 kernels occasionally increase per-token variance; their average is cheaper but p99 can be worse without warmup
[06:30] Samir: this is why we run mixed quant profiles; recommended: baseline in fp16 for p99 belt, enable int8 for throughput-only jobs or when you have strong evals
[06:48] John: can you describe kernel selection and how it relates to sequence length and MTU? we have occasionally seen fragmentation when grpc payloads cross an MTU boundary
[06:58] Priya: kernel selection is mostly about model layout and seq len. For long sequences some attention kernels are more efficient. MTU fragmentation affects networking stack — if your requests fragment you increase processing and reassembly on NAT which increases latency. Recommend using PMTU discovery or set MSS on your hosts to avoid fragmentation for typical packet sizes
[07:24] Rajesh: what about hairpin NAT and client IP preservation; we need logs for audit to show which internal tenant made the call
[07:33] Samir: with PrivateLink you get the ENI source, so you can preserve the internal IP in flow logs. With central nat you lose the original source IP unless you use proxy that injects an X-Forwarded-For header and we capture that in the control-plane logs
[07:55] John: we also wanted to test a scenario: we have a 70/30 split between real-time and batch; can you help run a perf sim with those ratios?
[08:05] Priya: yes, we can spin up a perf harness. ideal test: replay real traffic with a heatmap of key popularity to exercise hot keys. we'll measure p50/p95/p99, token throughput, and per-call CPU/GPU utilization
[08:25] Leah: any specific network metrics to collect?
[08:29] Priya: collect RTT histograms, retransmits, MTU fragmentation counts, tcp_sack events, and NAT translation table usage. also capture DNS latency and NXDOMAIN counts for split-horizon mistakes
[08:48] Samir: also capture cache metrics: hit/miss ratio per-key, evictions/sec, average KV read latency, and batch queue length over time
[09:05] John: how do we do canaries? we want slow rollouts without blowing up cost
[09:12] Priya: use targeted canaries: send e.g., 5% of traffic to a model variant with smaller quantization and smaller batch sizes. Redwood console supports route-based rollouts and automatic fallback if error or latency thresholds exceed
[09:30] Rajesh: security question on PrivateLink: does Redwood require opening inbound ports? we need to avoid inbound allowances
[09:38] Samir: no inbound open ports — PrivateLink uses ENIs and the connection is initiated from the client side; access is over vpc endpoint's interface. You can lock it down via security groups and resource-based policies
[09:55] Leah: what about DNS TTLs; if we change endpoints during a failover, will clients honor new IPs quickly enough?
[10:02] Priya: TTLs are important. We do a staged cutover pattern: lower TTL a few minutes ahead, update endpoint, then raise TTL. But some resolvers ignore small TTLs; that's why pre-warming and connection draining are also part of the runbook
[10:25] Samir: ok let's sketch the recommended topology: per-az compute + per-az nat for external internet egress, privatelink endpoints in each az for Redwood control plane and model pulls, route53 private hosted zone or conditional forwarder for DNS resolution, and per-az KV cache shards
[10:45] John: sounds good, cost wise what should we expect?
[10:50] Samir: per-az nat adds cost proportional to number of nat gateways plus data transfer; PrivateLink has fixed endpoint charges but reduces cross-az transfer; overall for your 3-AZ setup, estimate a 20-40% increase in infra cost but p99 halves in our sims — we sent a quick spreadsheet in chat
[11:10] Leah: if we accept higher infra cost is it reasonable to keep central nat for non-latency paths and only route inference traffic via privatelink?
[11:18] Priya: absolutely, route segmentation is typical: inference endpoints via privatelink and control plane; legacy services via central nat. Redwood's routing policy can tag traffic so you get cost/latency per-route breakdowns in the console
[11:40] John: could we do hybrid: privatelink for inference, nat for model registry updates which are less latency sensitive
[11:48] Samir: yes that's basically the recommended pattern
[12:00] Priya: one more note on KV eviction: if you have hot-key storms, it's helpful to implement request coalescing at app level and use a small 'spin' window on cache misses to avoid thundering herds
[12:15] John: what about library-level support? our engineers prefer we don't change app code much
[12:20] Priya: Redwood runtime has client-side SDKs that can help with coalescing and jittering; we can drop a snippet for your language
[12:30] Leah: any gotchas with on-prem hybrid? we plan a future air-gapped staging env
[12:36] Samir: on-prem requires a private control plane option or air-gapped package. Networking is trickier — you get to control MTU and switches which is good, but you must also run the KV plane and ensure low-latency interconnects
[12:52] Rajesh: last sec on compliance: we need proof of SOC2 logs and key rotation audit for the pilot
[12:58] Samir: we'll attach our SOC2 a3 report and a key rotation playbook. also we'll provide an architecture diagram with audit log locations
[13:10] Priya: ok let's confirm next steps; we'll schedule a bench run, share docs, and set a security call. any blockers?
[13:18] John: need to get sample traffic and a small team to run the replay
[13:22] Leah: i'll own the replay and send the distribution
[13:25] Samir: great. we'll follow up with a runbook link and a calendar invite for the bench run

Closing notes:
- Agreed topology: per-az compute and KV shards, privatelink endpoints per-az for inference traffic, optional per-az nat for internet egress
- Bench plan: 2 batch profiles (short/long), 70/30 real-time/batch, measure p50/p95/p99, token throughput, KV heatmap
- Docs to share: topology runbook, perf spreadsheet, SOC2 & key rotation playbook

References mentioned:
- perf spreadsheet link (shared in chat)
- topology runbook (to be shared by Samir)

End of transcript
